children: Wall Street's major averages were higher on Friday, as the S&P 500 (
led the rise in an attempt to recover from a persistent technology-led selloff.
Now, here are four news stories that broke in the morning to watch out for:
U.S. economy adds 165,000 jobs in October, crushing estimates: U.S. nonfarm payrolls

by 165,000 in October, more than double the 62,000 consensus and well above the 60,000 added in September, according to data released by the Bureau of Labor Statistics on Friday. The unemployment rate ticked down to 4.1% from 4.2%, even as the labor force participation rate edged up to 61.9%. The robust print, combined with upward revisions totaling 84,000 for August and September, prompted traders to raise the probability of a 25-basis-point Fed rate hike in December to 72.8% from 66.9% on Thursday.
Semiconductor and AI stocks bounce back following Thursday's steep selloff: The iShares Semiconductor ETF and VanEck Semiconductor ETF both

more than 3% on Friday, recovering from Thursday's sharp decline driven by concerns over tighter AI regulation following the Democratic win in the midterm elections. AMD rose approximately 10%, while Intel and Qualcomm both added 6%, and Nvidia gained more than 4% after plunging 9.26% in the previous session. Shares of data-center operators also recovered, with IREN surging 21% and Applied Digital gaining 7%.
Moderna shares rally on surprise Q3 profit and upgraded 2026 growth outlook: Moderna

shares  bounced back on Friday after the biotech reported Q3 revenue of $1.3 billion, with approximately 29% year-over-year growth beating consensus by $409.8 million, driven by improved COVID vaccine sales in international markets. Moderna raised its full-year revenue growth outlook to 15%–25%, up from up to 10% previously, and lowered its 2026 capital expenditure estimate to approximately $200 million.

Copper futures drop to lowest level since July amid AI spending and tariff uncertainty: London Metal Exchange three-month copper futures  fell as much as 1.5% to $13,630 per metric ton on Friday, putting the metal on track for a weekly loss of nearly 3%. The decline followed the Democratic sweep in the U.S. midterm elections, which triggered concerns over potential slowdowns in data center construction and reduced the prospect of expanded import tariffs. The U.S.-LME price differential has narrowed this week as traders reassess tariff risks.
